concepts.name: What history is and where evidence comes from
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Definition of history and why it is studied; types of history (social, political, economic, local, family); the main sources (archaeology and artefacts, written documents, oral tradition, pictures and photographs, buildings and sites) with the advantages and disadvantages of each; primary and secondary sources. Using sources as evidence in exam questions (reliability, bias, cross-referencing) is hist.skills.source-evaluation.

concepts.name: Using sources as historical evidence
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 3 'analyse sources' and the source-based question of Paper 1; Cambridge AO3 and Paper 2). Comprehension and inference from a written or visual source, provenance (who, when, why, for whom), purpose and message, reliability and bias, usefulness, comparing two sources (similarity and difference), checking a source against own knowledge and other sources, and reaching a judgement on how far sources support a claim. Practised on ORIGINAL invented sources only. The kinds of source and their general pros and cons are hist.intro.history-and-sources.

concepts.name: The origins of humankind and Africa as the cradle of humankind
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Theories of human origins (scientific theory of evolution and religious creation accounts, presented respectfully as different kinds of explanation), Charles Darwin and natural selection, stages of human development (Australopithecus, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Homo sapiens) in outline, why Africa is regarded as the cradle of humankind, and major sites (Olduvai Gorge, Taung, Sterkfontein, Laetoli, Hadar) with only well-established finds and dates given as approximate.

concepts.name: Ancient Egypt: the Nile, farming, achievements and legacy
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Meaning of civilisation; location of ancient Egypt and the importance of the Nile; government (pharaohs) and society in outline; agriculture (annual flood, basin irrigation, the shaduf, the three seasons and the calendar); science, medicine, mathematics and astronomy; religion and mummification; hieroglyphic writing and papyrus; architecture (pyramids, temples); the spread and influence of Egyptian civilisation on other parts of the world. Dates are approximate and given as BCE.

concepts.name: Stone Age and Early Iron Age societies in Zimbabwe
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Early, Middle and Late Stone Age tools and ways of life (hunting and gathering, the San and rock paintings), the arrival and spread of Early Iron Age farming communities (iron working, pottery, crops, livestock, villages), their social, economic and political organisation, and the changes from the Stone Age to the Early Iron Age. Dates as approximate ranges only.

concepts.name: Mapungubwe and the Great Zimbabwe state
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Mapungubwe as a forerunner (location, trade, social differentiation); the rise of Great Zimbabwe (factors such as cattle, gold and ivory trade with the coast, religion, leadership, location); political, economic, social and religious organisation; the stone buildings (Hill Complex, Great Enclosure) described accurately; theories about its decline (overpopulation and environmental exhaustion, shift of trade routes, succession disputes) presented as theories; the colonial-era myths that denied its African origin and how archaeology refuted them.

concepts.name: The Mutapa state
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Origins (Nyatsimba Mutota and the northward move, traditions presented as traditions), rise, political, economic (trade, tribute, gold, agriculture), social and religious organisation (mhondoro spirit mediums), relations with the Portuguese up to the seventeenth century in outline, and reasons for decline (civil wars, Portuguese interference, Rozvi rise). Detailed Portuguese activities and the prazo system are hist.contact.portuguese-prazos.

concepts.name: The Torwa and Rozvi states
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The Torwa (Butua) state and Khami in outline; the rise of the Rozvi under Changamire Dombo (expulsion of the Portuguese from the plateau in the 1690s), Danangombe (Dhlo Dhlo) and Naletale; political, economic, social and religious organisation; decline (succession disputes, drought, Nguni invasions in the 1830s).

concepts.name: The Mfecane and the Zulu state
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Meaning of Mfecane; causes (population and land pressure, drought, trade competition, the rise of strong states), Dingiswayo and the Mthethwa, Shaka's rise and military reforms (age regiments, the short stabbing spear, the cow-horn formation, discipline), the political, economic and social organisation of the Zulu state, effects of the Mfecane on southern and central Africa (including Nguni groups crossing Zimbabwe), and the decline of the Zulu state. Contested interpretations of the Mfecane presented as debates.

concepts.name: The Ndebele state
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Mzilikazi's break with Shaka, migration and settlement in south-western Zimbabwe (about 1838-1840), incorporation of conquered peoples, political organisation (king, izinduna, regiments), economic organisation (cattle, raiding and tribute, agriculture, trade), social organisation (Zansi, Enhla and Hole), Lobengula's reign, and the decline and fall of the state (1893-94 in outline; the war itself is hist.colonisation.anglo-ndebele-war).

concepts.name: Slavery and the slave trade in Africa: forms, causes and methods
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Forms of slavery (domestic or household slavery in African societies, chattel slavery, the slave trade), the trans-Saharan and East African (Indian Ocean) trades in outline, economic, social and political causes of the slave trade, and methods of obtaining slaves (raids, wars, kidnapping, debt and punishment, trade by African and foreign merchants). The Atlantic triangular trade is hist.slavery.atlantic-trade.

concepts.name: The triangular (Atlantic) slave trade
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Areas involved (Europe, West and West-Central Africa, the Americas and the Caribbean), the three legs and the goods exchanged on each, the Middle Passage and conditions on board, plantation slavery in the Americas in outline. Numbers only as widely accepted estimates (about 12 million Africans embarked, with many deaths at sea).

concepts.name: Effects of the slave trade on Africa and its abolition
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Negative and positive effects on the African continent (depopulation, insecurity and wars, decline of crafts and agriculture, rise of some states and merchants, new crops) with balance; groups that campaigned for abolition (humanitarians, Quakers, evangelical Christians, formerly enslaved writers, enslaved people's own resistance), economic and humanitarian reasons for abolition (including the debate about the Industrial Revolution), key dates (British abolition of the trade 1807 and of slavery 1833-34), and the challenges of ending the trade (naval patrols, continuing demand, the East African trade).

concepts.name: The Portuguese in the Zambezi valley and the prazo system
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Reasons for Portuguese penetration (gold, ivory, trade, Christianity, rivalry with Swahili-Arab traders), activities (trading fairs, Gonçalo da Silveira 1561, the Barreto expedition 1569-73, treaties with the Mutapa), relationships with Africans; the prazo system (crown land grants, prazeros, achikunda armies, characteristics) and its impact on Africans.

concepts.name: Early missionaries and European agents of colonisation
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Early missionary groups and areas of operation (London Missionary Society at Inyati 1859 and Hope Fountain, the Jesuit Zambezi Mission, later Dutch Reformed, Anglican and Methodist missions), missionary activities (evangelism, schools, health, agriculture), challenges faced, impact on African societies; European agents of colonisation (missionaries, hunters, traders, explorers such as Livingstone, concession seekers) and their role in preparing the way for colonisation.

concepts.name: The Scramble for southern Africa and the Berlin Conference
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Countries involved in the scramble for and partition of southern Africa (Britain, Portugal, Germany, the Boer republics), its causes (economic, political, strategic, social and religious motives), reasons for convening the Berlin Conference (1884-85), countries that attended, its resolutions (effective occupation, notification, spheres of influence, free navigation, suppression of the slave trade) and the effects of partition. General imperialism theory for Cambridge is hist.imperialism.motives.

concepts.name: The colonisation of Zimbabwe: treaties, concessions and occupation
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Countries in the scramble for Zimbabwe; reasons for colonisation (the 'second Rand' gold myth, Rhodes's Cape-to-Cairo ambitions, land, strategic rivalry); the Grobler Treaty (1887), Moffat Treaty (1888) and Rudd Concession (1888) and Lobengula's response; the Royal Charter (1889) and the British South Africa Company; the Pioneer Column and the occupation of Mashonaland (1890, Fort Salisbury).

concepts.name: The Anglo-Ndebele War, 1893-94
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Causes (the Victoria incident, Company ambitions and the need for land and gold, border raids, Jameson's plans), the course of the war (Shangani and Bembesi, the fall of Bulawayo, Lobengula's flight, the Shangani Patrol), and the results for the Ndebele (loss of land and cattle, reserves, forced labour) and for the Company.

concepts.name: The First Chimurenga/Umvukela, 1896-97
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Causes (land and cattle seizures, forced labour, hut tax, brutality of the Native Police, natural disasters such as rinderpest, drought and locusts, the Jameson Raid), the course of the risings in Matabeleland and Mashonaland, the role of chiefs and spirit mediums (Mkwati, Kaguvi, Nehanda and others), reasons for defeat, and results (including the execution of Kaguvi and Nehanda in 1898 and changes in Company administration). Interpretations of coordination between the risings presented as a historians' debate.

concepts.name: Company rule in Southern Rhodesia, 1890-1923
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Features of BSAC administration (administrator, Legislative Council from 1898, Native Affairs Department), political, economic and social policies (land alienation and reserves, hut tax, labour recruitment, mining and settler farming), African responses, and the reasons Company rule ended (financial problems, settler pressure, the 1922 referendum).

concepts.name: Responsible Government, 1923-1953
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Meaning of Responsible Government and why it was granted in 1923; its features; its political, economic and social policies (Land Apportionment Act 1930, Maize Control Act 1931, Industrial Conciliation Act 1934, Native Land Husbandry Act 1951, segregation in towns, education and health) and their impact on indigenous people; early African associations and protest in outline. Dates of acts as given here; other detail only if certain.

concepts.name: The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, 1953-1963
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Reasons for federation (economic, political and strategic, settler and British motives) and African opposition; steps towards it (conferences, the 1953 referendum); policies and developments (partnership, Kariba Dam, economic growth and its distribution); successes and failures; reasons for collapse (African nationalism in Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia, the 1959 emergency, the Monckton Commission, British policy) and dissolution on 31 December 1963.

concepts.name: UDI and Rhodesia, 1965-1979
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Reasons for the Unilateral Declaration of Independence (11 November 1965) by Ian Smith's Rhodesian Front; British and international reactions (sanctions, NIBMAR, the Tiger and Fearless talks, the Pearce Commission 1972); policies and developments during UDI (1969 constitution, Land Tenure Act 1969, republic 1970, sanctions-busting, protected villages) and their impact on the indigenous people. The liberation war itself is hist.liberation.*.

concepts.name: Pan-Africanism and the rise of mass nationalism in Africa
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Definition and aims of Pan-Africanism, reasons for its rise, the roles of W. E. B. Du Bois and Marcus Garvey, the Pan-African Congresses (1919-1945, Manchester 1945) and Kwame Nkrumah in outline; meaning of mass nationalism and the causes of its rise in Africa after the Second World War (war experience, education, urbanisation, colonial grievances, the UN and the Atlantic Charter, independence of India and Ghana). Zimbabwe's own nationalist movements are hist.liberation.nationalist-movements.

concepts.name: Mass nationalism in Zimbabwe, 1957-1964
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The City Youth League, the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress (1957), the National Democratic Party (1960), ZAPU (1961) and ZANU (1963): leaders, aims, activities (rallies, strikes, boycotts, petitions) and the challenges they faced (bans, detentions, divisions, restrictive laws), treated with balance and without partisan judgement.

concepts.name: The turn to armed struggle and its early phase, 1964-1970
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Causes of the armed struggle and reasons for the move from peaceful politics (bans, detentions, failed negotiations, UDI, land); recruitment strategies and countries where freedom fighters trained (e.g. Tanzania, Zambia, Ghana, Algeria, the USSR, China); the early battles (Chinhoyi, 28 April 1966; Hwange (Wankie) and Sipolilo, 1967-68, with the ANC of South Africa) and reasons for the failure of the early phase (conventional tactics, lack of mass support and intelligence, Rhodesian and South African forces).

concepts.name: The second phase of the armed struggle, 1972-1979, and the role of the masses
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Change of strategy (guerrilla warfare, politicisation of peasants), the opening of the north-eastern front (Altena Farm, December 1972), bases in Mozambique after 1975 and Zambia, ZANLA and ZIPRA, main events including raids on camps (Nyadzonia 1976, Chimoio 1977, Freedom Camp 1978) described factually and respectfully; the role of the masses (peasants, mujibhas and chimbwidos, chiefs, spirit mediums, churches) and of international organisations; Rhodesian counter-measures in outline.

concepts.name: Attempts at a settlement and the Lancaster House agreement
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Détente and the Victoria Falls conference (1975), the Geneva conference (1976), the Internal Settlement (March 1978) and Zimbabwe-Rhodesia (1979), the Lancaster House Conference (September-December 1979) and its agreement (constitution, ceasefire, transition), and why each attempt failed or succeeded.

concepts.name: Independence (1980) and the policy of reconciliation
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Events leading to independence (ceasefire, return of refugees and combatants, the February 1980 elections), independence on 18 April 1980, the policy of reconciliation (aims, examples, achievements and limits) and the integration of the armies, presented factually.

concepts.name: Social, political and economic developments since 1980
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Social policies (expansion of education and health, women's rights such as the Legal Age of Majority Act 1982, recreation and sport), economic policies (growth with equity, job creation, the Economic Structural Adjustment Programme from 1991 and its effects, later economic challenges described without disputed statistics), political developments (the disturbances in Matabeleland and the Midlands in the 1980s, known as Gukurahundi, acknowledged factually and sensitively; the Unity Accord of 22 December 1987; the executive presidency; later political developments in neutral outline). Land reform and foreign policy are separate concepts.

concepts.name: Land reform and indigenisation
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The land question at independence, phases of land reform (willing-buyer willing-seller in the 1980s-90s, the fast-track programme from 2000), aims, the role of the Constitution in land redistribution, the reaction of Western countries, recognised benefits and problems; indigenisation and economic empowerment policies and measures for gender equity. Balanced: aims, outcomes and criticisms, no slogans.

concepts.name: Zimbabwe and the international community since 1980
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Principles of Zimbabwe's foreign policy, relations with the European Union and Western countries (sanctions and restrictive measures from the early 2000s, presented with the different views on them), the Look East Policy and relations with China, and peacekeeping and peacemaking (Mozambique in the 1980s, UN missions, the DRC from 1998).

concepts.name: The Frontline States and external support for the liberation struggle
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Members of the Frontline States (formed in the 1970s; Tanzania, Zambia, Botswana, Mozambique, Angola, and Zimbabwe after 1980), their aims and role in the liberation of Zimbabwe (bases, diplomacy, pressure in negotiations) and the costs they bore; support from other countries and organisations (OAU Liberation Committee, the USSR, China, Cuba, the UN and sanctions) in outline.

concepts.name: SADCC and SADC
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Origins (SADCC 1980, SADC 1992), member states, aims, structure in outline, the role of SADC in the socio-economic development of the region, and its successes and failures.

concepts.name: The OAU and the African Union
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Origins of the OAU (Addis Ababa, 25 May 1963), aims, principal organs and their functions, its social, economic and political work (including the Liberation Committee), successes and failures; transformation into the African Union (2002), its aims and organs and an assessment.

concepts.name: The Commonwealth and the Non-Aligned Movement
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Commonwealth: origins, aims, activities, functions of its organs, Zimbabwe's membership and withdrawal (2003); Non-Aligned Movement: origins (Bandung 1955, Belgrade 1961), aims, activities, the Harare summit (1986).

concepts.name: The United Nations
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Formation (1945) and aims, structure and functions of the main organs (General Assembly, Security Council and the veto, Secretariat, International Court of Justice, Economic and Social Council, specialised agencies), the work and effectiveness of the UN (peacekeeping, development, humanitarian work), and its role in promoting and protecting human rights (the Universal Declaration of Human Rights 1948).

concepts.name: The Constitution of Zimbabwe
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Definition and functions of a constitution; the Constitution of Zimbabwe (2013) in outline: citizenship, the Declaration of Rights, the functions of the executive, legislature and judiciary and the separation of powers. Accurate, general description; no section numbers unless certain.

concepts.name: Democracy
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Meaning and principles of democracy (popular participation, free and fair elections, rule of law, separation of powers, accountability, freedom of expression), types (direct, representative, parliamentary, presidential), and how government has promoted democracy in Zimbabwe, discussed in a balanced way.

concepts.name: Human rights and children's rights and responsibilities
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Human rights as set out in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and the Constitution of Zimbabwe, children's rights and responsibilities (as in the Constitution and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child), limitations on some rights, and government efforts to promote human and children's rights.

concepts.name: The Chinese Revolution to 1949
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Causes (the end of the Qing dynasty in 1911-12, warlords, foreign domination, peasant poverty), the Guomindang and the Communist Party, the struggle between them from 1925 to 1949 (the 1927 split, the Jiangxi Soviet, the Long March 1934-35, war with Japan, the civil war), how the Communists won peasant support and the role of the peasants, and why the Communists won (People's Republic proclaimed 1 October 1949).

concepts.name: China under Mao Zedong, 1949-1976
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Political, social and economic problems in 1949 and how the Communists dealt with them: land reform, the First Five-Year Plan, the Hundred Flowers campaign, the Great Leap Forward and the famine (deaths given as historians' estimates), the Cultural Revolution, social changes (women, education, health); assessment of Mao's rule with its achievements and very high human costs.

concepts.name: The Cuban Revolution
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The nature of the Batista regime, Fidel Castro and the 26th of July Movement (Moncada 1953, the Granma landing 1956, the Sierra Maestra campaign), the victory of January 1959, the stages of the revolution and its domestic results, and its effects on the world (alignment with the USSR, support for liberation movements in Africa and Latin America) in outline. US reactions and the Missile Crisis are hist.containment.cuba.

concepts.name: Fascism, Nazism and Mussolini's Italy
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Meaning and features of fascism and Nazism; inter-war problems in Italy and Germany that favoured dictatorship (war debts, unemployment, weak governments, fear of communism, resentment of the peace settlement); Mussolini's rise (March on Rome, 1922), his domestic policies (the corporate state, the Lateran Treaty, propaganda, repression) and foreign policy (Corfu 1923, Abyssinia 1935-36, the Axis). Hitler's rise and rule are the shared hist.germany.* concepts.

concepts.name: The First World War, 1914-1918: course and results (overview)
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Overview of the main fronts and events (the Western Front and trench warfare, the Eastern Front, the war at sea, Gallipoli, the war in Africa including East Africa and the participation of Rhodesians and Africans, the entry of the USA, the armistice of 11 November 1918) and the political, economic and social consequences of the war. Cambridge Depth study A goes deeper (hist.ww1.*).

concepts.name: The Second World War, 1939-1945: course and results (overview)
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Overview of the main campaigns and turning points (Blitzkrieg and the fall of France, the Battle of Britain, Operation Barbarossa and Stalingrad, North Africa, Pearl Harbor and the Pacific, D-Day, the defeat of Germany and Japan), African and Rhodesian participation, and the results of the war (casualties as approximate figures, the UN, superpowers, decolonisation, the Cold War). Cambridge Depth study E goes deeper (hist.ww2.*).

concepts.name: Manifestations and impact of the Cold War (overview)
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Meaning of the Cold War; its manifestations (alliances, the arms and space races, propaganda, crises over Berlin and Cuba, proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Angola and elsewhere) and its impact on the world, including Africa (support for rival liberation movements and governments), to the end of the Cold War (1989-91) in outline. The origins to 1949 are the shared hist.cold-war.* concepts.

concepts.name: Why there were so many revolutions in 1848
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Liberalism and nationalism and why they had grown by 1848, the Metternich system, economic crisis (harvest failures, unemployment), the spread of revolution from Paris, and what the revolutions had in common. The events in Italy and Germany are taught with unification (hist.italy.before-1850, hist.german-unification.before-1851).

concepts.name: The 1848 revolutions in France and the Austrian Empire, and why most failed
concepts.description: Cambridge only. France (February 1848, the Second Republic, the June Days, Louis Napoleon's election); the Austrian Empire (Vienna and the fall of Metternich, Hungary and Kossuth, Prague, the role of the army and Russian intervention, Franz Joseph); reasons for the failure of the revolutions across Europe and what they changed (end of serfdom in Austria, constitutions, lessons for nationalists).

concepts.name: Italy before 1850: Austrian influence, Mazzini and 1848-49
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The divided peninsula after 1815 and Austrian influence, Italian nationalism and Mazzini (Young Italy), the events of 1848-49 (risings, Charles Albert's war, Custoza and Novara, the Roman Republic) and why Italy was not unified in 1848-49.

concepts.name: Cavour, Victor Emmanuel II and the war of 1859
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Piedmont under Victor Emmanuel II and Cavour (modernisation, the Crimean War, diplomacy), the agreement of Plombières (1858), the war with Austria in 1859 (Magenta, Solferino, Villafranca), the annexation of the central duchies, and whether Cavour helped or hindered unification.

concepts.name: Garibaldi and the completion of Italian unification
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Garibaldi's expedition of the Thousand to Sicily and Naples (1860), relations with Cavour, the meeting at Teano, the Kingdom of Italy (1861), Venetia (1866) and Rome (1870), the importance of Garibaldi's contribution and of other European countries in Italian unification.

concepts.name: German nationalism, the Zollverein and 1848-50
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The German Confederation, German nationalism, the Zollverein, the 1848 revolution in Prussia, the Frankfurt Parliament and its failure, and the re-establishment of Austrian influence by 1850 (Olmütz); why Germany was not unified in 1848-50.

concepts.name: Bismarck and the defeat of Austria, 1862-1866
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Bismarck as Minister-President (1862), the army reforms and the constitutional crisis, Schleswig-Holstein (1864, Gastein), the Austro-Prussian War (1866) and its consequences (North German Confederation).

concepts.name: Bismarck, France and the creation of the German Empire, 1866-1871
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Relations with France, the Hohenzollern candidature for the Spanish throne and the Ems telegram, the Franco-Prussian War (1870-71), the proclamation of the German Empire (18 January 1871), and how far Bismarck was responsible for unification (with the roles of economic power, nationalism and the mistakes of others).

concepts.name: Causes of the American Civil War, 1820-1861
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Differences between North and South, slavery, slave and free states (Missouri Compromise 1820, Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act 1854, Dred Scott 1857), abolitionism, the 1860 election and the significance of Lincoln's victory, secession and Fort Sumter (April 1861); how far slavery caused the war.

concepts.name: The Civil War, 1861-1865: why the North won
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Resources of each side, strategy and key turning points in outline (Antietam, Gettysburg, Vicksburg, Sherman's march), the Emancipation Proclamation (1863) and Black soldiers, the role of Lincoln, and the reasons for the North's victory and the South's defeat.

concepts.name: Reconstruction, 1865-1877
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The aims of Reconstruction, the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments, the Freedmen's Bureau, Black Codes and the Ku Klux Klan, Radical Reconstruction, the end of Reconstruction (1877) and the extent of its success; did the war change anything.

concepts.name: Motives for European and US imperialism
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Economic, military, geopolitical, religious and cultural motives for nineteenth-century imperialism (raw materials, markets, investment, strategic bases, prestige and nationalism, missionary activity, ideas of racial superiority presented critically), with examples from Europe and the USA.

concepts.name: French and British rule in Africa: Senegal and Nigeria
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The French model of assimilation and direct rule (Faidherbe and Senegal) and the British model of indirect rule (Lugard and Nigeria): how each worked and their varied impacts on Africans, compared.

concepts.name: Leopold II and the Congo Free State
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Leopold II and private imperialism, the Congo Free State (1885-1908), rubber and the forced-labour system, atrocities and the international campaign against them, and the Belgian takeover in 1908; impact on the people of the Congo. Death tolls as historians' estimates, presented with care.

concepts.name: The British in India and the events of 1857
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The East India Company, causes of the 1857 rising (named by different traditions as a mutiny, rebellion or first war of independence), its course and suppression, and the changes it brought to British rule (Government of India Act 1858, the Raj).

concepts.name: The Spanish-American War and US imperialism, 1898-1906
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Wars of independence in Cuba and the Philippines, the Spanish-American War (1898) and the Treaty of Paris, the debate in the USA over imperialism, the Philippine-American War and the consequences of American control for Filipinos, and American intervention in Cuba to 1906 (the Platt Amendment).

concepts.name: The alliance system and the arms race, 1890-1914
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC causes of the First World War; Cambridge Option A key question 6). The Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente (Franco-Russian Alliance 1894, Entente Cordiale 1904, Anglo-Russian Entente 1907), the Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902), European diplomacy, the naval race (Dreadnoughts) and military planning; whether alliances made war more or less likely.

concepts.name: Colonial rivalries and the Balkans, 1890-1914
concepts.description: Both boards. Colonial rivalries and crises between the Great Powers (Moroccan crises 1905-06 and 1911, Fashoda 1898 in outline), the decline of the Ottoman Empire, Serbian and Slav nationalism, the Bosnian crisis (1908-09) and the Balkan Wars (1912-13), and why Balkan problems were so hard to solve.

concepts.name: The July Crisis and the outbreak of war, 1914
concepts.description: Both boards. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand (28 June 1914), the 'blank cheque', the Austrian ultimatum to Serbia, mobilisations, the Schlieffen Plan and Belgian neutrality, the declarations of war (28 July-4 August 1914), and the debate about responsibility for the war (presented as a historians' debate).

concepts.name: The peacemakers of 1919 and their aims
concepts.description: Both boards. The aims and roles of Wilson (the Fourteen Points), Clemenceau and Lloyd George, their disagreements and compromises, why the victors did not get everything they wanted, and contemporary opinions about whether the settlement could be justified.

concepts.name: The Treaty of Versailles and its impact on Germany to 1923
concepts.description: Both boards. The terms of the Treaty (territory, military, reparations, war guilt, the League), the other treaties in outline (St Germain, Trianon, Neuilly, Sèvres), German reactions ('Diktat'), and the social, economic and political impact on Germany to the end of 1923, linked to the debate on whether the Treaty was fair. The Weimar crises in depth are hist.germany.weimar-1918-23.

concepts.name: The League of Nations: aims, structure and membership
concepts.description: Both boards. The Covenant and aims (collective security, disarmament, cooperation), structure and functions of the organs (Assembly, Council, Secretariat, Permanent Court, commissions and agencies such as the ILO), membership (the absence of the USA, Germany and the USSR at first), sanctions, and how far weaknesses made failure inevitable.

concepts.name: The League in the 1920s: peacekeeping and humanitarian work
concepts.description: Both boards. Successes and failures in peacekeeping (Vilna 1920, the Aaland Islands 1920-21, Corfu 1923, Bulgaria 1925) and the humanitarian work of its agencies (refugees, health, working conditions, slavery), with an assessment of their importance.

concepts.name: The League in the 1930s: Depression, Manchuria and Abyssinia
concepts.description: Both boards. How the Depression made the League's work harder, the causes, events and consequences of the Manchurian crisis (1931-33) and the Abyssinian crisis (1935-36), and the reasons for the League's collapse by 1939.

concepts.name: Hitler's aims and early foreign policy, 1933-1936
concepts.description: Both boards. Hitler's foreign policy aims (overturning Versailles, uniting German speakers, Lebensraum, anti-communism), rearmament and conscription (1935), the Saar plebiscite (1935), the remilitarisation of the Rhineland (1936), the Rome-Berlin Axis and the Anti-Comintern Pact, and German and Italian involvement in the Spanish Civil War.

concepts.name: Anschluss, Czechoslovakia and appeasement, 1938
concepts.description: Both boards. The Anschluss with Austria (March 1938), the crisis over the Sudetenland and the Munich Agreement (September 1938), the policy of appeasement (Chamberlain's reasons, arguments for and against) and whether it was justified.

concepts.name: The outbreak of war in 1939: who was to blame?
concepts.description: Both boards. The occupation of Czechoslovakia (March 1939), the British guarantee to Poland, the Nazi-Soviet Pact (23 August 1939), the invasion of Poland and the British and French declarations of war (3 September 1939); weighing Hitler's policy against the Treaty of Versailles, the League's failures, appeasement and the Pact as causes.

concepts.name: The breakdown of the wartime alliance, 1945-1946
concepts.description: Both boards. Ideological differences between the USA and the USSR, the Yalta and Potsdam conferences (1945), the atomic bomb, and the breakdown of the alliance in 1945-46 (Kennan's 'Long Telegram' and Churchill's 'Iron Curtain' speech mentioned and paraphrased).

concepts.name: Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe and the American response, 1945-1948
concepts.description: Both boards. How the USSR gained control of Eastern Europe by 1948 (occupation, 'salami tactics', Czechoslovakia 1948, Cominform), American reactions (containment, the Truman Doctrine 1947, Marshall Aid), and Soviet responses.

concepts.name: Germany, the Berlin Blockade and who was to blame for the Cold War
concepts.description: Both boards. The occupation of Germany, the Berlin Blockade and airlift (1948-49) and its consequences (two German states 1949), NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955), and the debate over whether the USA or the USSR was more to blame (traditional, revisionist and post-revisionist views in outline).

concepts.name: The United States and Korea, 1950-1953
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Background (division of Korea 1945), North Korea's invasion of South Korea (June 1950), American reactions and the involvement of the UN, the course of the war (Inchon, the Chinese intervention, stalemate, armistice 1953) and how far containment succeeded.

concepts.name: The United States and Cuba, 1959-1962
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC covers it with the Cuban Revolution). American reactions to the Cuban Revolution, the Bay of Pigs (1961), the Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962): causes, events, decisions of Kennedy and Khrushchev, its resolution and aftermath (hotline, Test Ban Treaty).

concepts.name: American involvement in Vietnam, 1955-1975
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Reasons for American involvement (domino theory, support for South Vietnam), escalation (Gulf of Tonkin 1964), tactics and strategy on both sides (search and destroy, bombing, chemical weapons, Viet Cong guerrilla warfare), the Tet Offensive (1968), opposition at home, reasons for withdrawal (Paris Peace Accords 1973) and the fall of Saigon (1975).

concepts.name: Hungary 1956 and Czechoslovakia 1968
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Soviet control of Eastern Europe after 1948, causes of opposition in Hungary (1956, Nagy) and Czechoslovakia (1968, Dubček and the Prague Spring), the Soviet reactions and the Brezhnev Doctrine, and the similarities and differences between the two.

concepts.name: The Berlin Wall, 1961
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The problem of Berlin, emigration from East Germany, why the Wall was built in August 1961, reactions (Kennedy's visit 1963), and its significance until 1989.

concepts.name: Solidarity and the collapse of Soviet control, 1980-1991
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Solidarity in Poland (1980-81, Wałęsa, martial law, 1989 elections), Gorbachev's reforms and the abandonment of the Brezhnev Doctrine, the revolutions of 1989 and the fall of the Berlin Wall (9 November 1989), and how far Gorbachev was personally responsible for the collapse of Soviet control.

concepts.name: The Schlieffen Plan and the coming of stalemate, 1914
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The Schlieffen Plan and how it worked in practice (the advance through Belgium, the British Expeditionary Force, Russian mobilisation), the battles of Mons and the Marne, the race to the sea and the First Battle of Ypres, and why a defensive war of attrition emerged by the end of 1914.

concepts.name: Trench warfare, new weapons, Verdun and the Somme
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Living and fighting in the trenches, the nature and problems of trench warfare, the use and impact of machine guns, gas, tanks and aircraft, the battles of Verdun and the Somme (1916) and the leadership and tactics of Haig (a debated reputation presented as such).

concepts.name: A world war: empire troops, Africa, Japan and the Arab Revolt
concepts.description: Cambridge only. British Empire troops on the Western Front (Indian and Canadian case studies), the war in Africa (German East Africa and South West Africa, including Indian and South African troops and African carriers), Japan's contribution (the siege of Tsingtao, protecting sea lanes) and the Arab Revolt.

concepts.name: The war at sea, Gallipoli, the Eastern Front and civilians
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The war at sea (Jutland, the U-boat campaign, convoys), the Gallipoli campaign (1915) and why it failed, events on the Eastern Front and the defeat of Russia, and the impact of the war on civilian populations.

concepts.name: Why Germany asked for an armistice in 1918
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The importance of American entry into the war (1917), the German Spring Offensive of 1918 and why it failed, the Allied advance, conditions in Germany (blockade, the Kiel mutiny, revolution, the Kaiser's abdication) and the Armistice of 11 November 1918.

concepts.name: The Weimar Republic, 1918-1923
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The revolution of 1918 and the establishment of the Republic, the Weimar Constitution and its strengths and weaknesses, political divisions and the army, German reactions to Versailles, threats from left and right (Spartacists 1919, Kapp Putsch 1920), the occupation of the Ruhr and hyperinflation (1923).

concepts.name: Recovery under Stresemann, 1924-1929
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Stresemann's economic achievements (the Rentenmark, the Dawes and Young Plans) and foreign policy (Locarno 1925, League membership 1926), cultural achievements of the Weimar period, and how far the Republic recovered.

concepts.name: The rise of the Nazis, 1919-1933
concepts.description: Both boards. Nazi ideas and methods, the Munich Putsch (1923) and its consequences, the roles of Hitler and other leaders, why the Nazis had little success before 1930, the impact of the Depression (1930-33), reasons for the Nazis' rise and how Hitler became Chancellor (30 January 1933).

concepts.name: Consolidation and control: the Nazi regime, 1933-1945
concepts.description: Both boards. The Reichstag Fire and the March 1933 election, the Enabling Act, the Night of the Long Knives, the death of Hindenburg (1934), the removal of opposition, methods of control and repression (SS, Gestapo, courts, camps), the use of culture and the mass media, opposition to Nazi rule, and whether Nazi Germany was a totalitarian state.

concepts.name: Life in Nazi Germany: economy, women and young people
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Economic policy (public works, autarky, rearmament, the Labour Front), whether most people benefited, policies towards women and the family, young people (Hitler Youth, schools, non-conformist groups), and how the coming of war and the war economy changed life.

concepts.name: Persecution and the Final Solution
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Nazi racial ideas, anti-Semitism and the persecution of Jews (boycott 1933, Nuremberg Laws 1935, Kristallnacht 1938), the persecution of other minorities (Roma and Sinti, disabled people, homosexual men, Jehovah's Witnesses), and the Final Solution during the war; taught accurately and with respect for victims (no graphic detail; figures as historians' estimates such as about six million Jews murdered).

concepts.name: Tsarist Russia and the 1905 Revolution
concepts.description: Both boards. The main features of Tsarist rule and Russian society before 1914, problems of ruling Russia, the 1905 Revolution (Bloody Sunday, the October Manifesto) and how the Tsar survived it, attempts at reform (the Dumas, Stolypin).

concepts.name: The revolutions of 1917
concepts.description: Both boards. The impact of the First World War on Russia, the March (February) Revolution of 1917 and the Tsar's abdication, the Provisional Government and the Soviets, reasons for the failure of the Provisional Government, and the Bolshevik seizure of power in November (October) 1917 and the role of Lenin. Explains the two calendars.

concepts.name: Bolshevik rule, the Civil War and the NEP, 1917-1924
concepts.description: Both boards. Early Bolshevik decrees and the Constituent Assembly, the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the Civil War and War Communism and reasons for Bolshevik victory, the Kronstadt Rising and the New Economic Policy (1921) and how far it succeeded, Lenin's death (1924).

concepts.name: Stalin's rise and dictatorship
concepts.description: Both boards. The struggle for power after Lenin's death and why Stalin, not Trotsky, emerged by 1928; Stalin's dictatorship (terror, the Purges and show trials, the Gulag, propaganda and the cult of personality, official culture) and how complete his control was by 1941. Death figures as historians' estimates.

concepts.name: Stalin's economic policies and life in the Soviet Union
concepts.description: Both boards. Reasons for and features of the Five-Year Plans and collectivisation, their successes and failures (including the famine of 1932-33 with estimates presented as such), and how different social groups, ethnic minorities and women were affected.

concepts.name: The US economic boom of the 1920s
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Factors behind the boom (government policies: laissez-faire, tariffs, low taxes; mass production, the motor car and consumer goods; credit and hire purchase; advertising), industries that prospered and older industries that did not, the decline of agriculture, who did not benefit, and weaknesses in the economy by the late 1920s.

concepts.name: The Roaring Twenties: society, culture and women
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The 'Roaring Twenties' (jazz, film and other media, sport), the changing roles of women (the vote 1920, flappers, work), Prohibition (1920) and gangsterism, and why Prohibition was repealed (1933).

concepts.name: Intolerance in 1920s America
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Restrictions on immigration (quota acts 1921 and 1924), the Red Scare and the Sacco and Vanzetti case, religious intolerance (the Scopes trial 1925), discrimination against Black Americans and the Ku Klux Klan, and how widespread intolerance was.

concepts.name: The Wall Street Crash, the Depression and the 1932 election
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Causes of the Wall Street Crash (October 1929; speculation, buying on the margin, overproduction, banking weaknesses), its financial, economic and social effects (unemployment, Hoovervilles), President Hoover's reaction, and why Roosevelt won the 1932 election (Hoover's and Roosevelt's programmes).

concepts.name: The New Deal: the Hundred Days and after
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Roosevelt's inauguration (March 1933), the Hundred Days, the alphabet agencies and their work (e.g. CCC, AAA, TVA, NRA, PWA, later WPA and the Social Security Act 1935), and how the character of the New Deal changed after 1933 (the Second New Deal).

concepts.name: Opposition to the New Deal and its success
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Opposition from Republicans, the rich, business interests, the Supreme Court and radical critics such as Huey Long, why unemployment persisted (the 1937-38 recession), and the strengths and weaknesses of the New Deal in dealing with unemployment and the Depression.

concepts.name: The war in Europe, 1939-1943: from Blitzkrieg to Stalingrad
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The extent of German conquest by 1940 (the invasion and surrender of France, Dunkirk, the Vichy government), German plans to invade Britain (Operation Sea Lion), the Battle of Britain and its consequences, why Hitler invaded the USSR (Operation Barbarossa, 1941) and its initial successes, and the German defeat at Stalingrad (1942-43) as a turning point.

concepts.name: The war in the Asia-Pacific, 1941-1942
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The deterioration of US-Japanese relations, the reasons for and consequences of the attack on Pearl Harbor (7 December 1941), reasons for initial Japanese successes in Southeast Asia (case study: Malaya and Singapore, February 1942), and the Battle of Midway (June 1942) as a turning point.

concepts.name: Civilians under bombing and occupation, and resistance
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The impact of bombing on people's lives and morale (the Blitz 1940-41; Allied bombing of German cities 1943-45), the impact of Japanese control on people's lives (case study: Malaya and Singapore), and the methods and effectiveness of resistance movements in Malaya and in France. Occupied Poland and the Holocaust are hist.ww2.occupied-poland-holocaust.

concepts.name: Nazi-occupied Poland and the Holocaust
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Nazi rule in occupied Europe with Poland as the case study (division of Poland, terror against Poles, ghettos), the circumstances leading to the Holocaust, the death camps and its impact; taught accurately, without graphic detail, with respect for victims and with figures as historians' estimates (about six million Jews murdered).

concepts.name: Allied victory in Europe, 1943-1945
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The Allied invasion of Sicily and the campaign in Italy, the D-Day landings (6 June 1944) and the advance to Germany, the Soviet advance from the east, and why Nazi Germany was on the point of collapse by April 1945 (surrender in May 1945).

concepts.name: The defeat of Japan and the consolidation of victory
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Guadalcanal and Okinawa, the US strategy of island-hopping, the bombing of Japan, the decision to use the atomic bomb (Hiroshima 6 August and Nagasaki 9 August 1945) and its consequences (a debated decision presented with different views), Japan's surrender; the Allied occupations of Germany and Japan and the war crimes trials at Nuremberg and Tokyo.
